name: HAA299

lead: HAA299 is an experimental organic filter designed to absorb long-wave UVA (UVA-1) and the violet edge of visible light. Those wavelengths reach deep into skin and are linked to aging and pigmentation, so the payoff is less deep UV damage and less light-induced darkening.

It absorbs light at the boundary between ultraviolet and visible wavelengths, which can trigger pigmentation through oxidative stress. A small volunteer study reported protection against pigmentation induced at 385 and 405 nm, and the EU's SCCS issued an opinion on a nano form in 2021.

paras: It is intended for sunscreen products, particularly those targeting long-wave UVA and visible-edge light. It is not established as a marketed consumer ingredient in the sources reviewed, and benefits for aging would build over long-term use.
Human evidence is limited to a single small pigmentation study, and there are no long-term appearance trials. Safety was assessed by the SCCS for the nano form only; details are in the full opinion.

angle.text: HAA299 is an experimental sunscreen filter designed to cover long-wave UVA-1 and the violet edge of visible light, wavelengths linked to skin aging and pigmentation. It has a small early study and an EU safety-committee opinion.

lead: HAA299, with the INCI name bis-(diethylaminohydroxybenzoyl benzoyl) piperazine, is an organic UV filter designed for sunscreens that absorbs long-wave UVA-1 radiation, and it is described as most effective when milled to a smaller particle size [1]. It matters for appearance because solar ultraviolet radiation drives skin pigmentation, and visible light has also been shown to cause rapid pigmentation, a process linked to oxidative stress, photoageing and skin cancer [2]. A filter that covers the longer wavelengths is aimed at keeping skin tone even and limiting the dark marks and ageing that sun exposure produces.

The substance has been reviewed by regulators rather than sold widely. The EU's Scientific Committee on Consumer Safety (SCCS) first gave an opinion on the non-nano form (SCCS/1533/14) and issued a second opinion on the nano form (SCCS/1634/21) in 2021 [1][3]. The UK's Scientific Advisory Group on Chemical Safety concluded in 2022 that both forms can be considered safe up to 10 percent, excluding spray and aerosol products [4].
A 2022 study reported that a visible-light-absorbing organic filter offered superior protection against pigmentation induced by wavelengths at the boundary between ultraviolet and visible light [2].

paras: HAA299 is intended as a sunscreen active against UVA-1 radiation, and the SCCS opinion describes it as designed to give consumers stronger UV protection and as most effective when milled to a smaller particle size [1]. Its sunscreen role is to absorb light before it reaches skin cells.

Solar UV radiation (about 295 to 400 nm) is well established as causing skin pigmentation, and visible light (400 to 740 nm) induces rapid pigmentation that is thought to be caused by oxidative stress; the UV-visible boundary region has been less well studied [2].

According to the SCCS, a dossier from industry to support the safe use of HAA299 was received by the European Commission in 2009 and was supplemented in 2012; the earlier opinion SCCS/1533/14 addressed the non-nano form and did not cover inhalation exposure [1][3]. The Commission asked the SCCS on 2 November 2020 to assess the nano form at up to 10 percent, and the committee adopted a preliminary opinion on 22 July 2021 and a final opinion on 26 to 27 October 2021 (SCCS/1634/21) [1][3].

The UK Scientific Advisory Group on Chemical Safety (SAG-CS) published its final opinion on HAA299 and HAA299 (nano) in September 2022. It noted that the applicant provided no data for concentrations above 10 percent but enough data to assess risk at up to 10 percent, that both forms are of low aqueous solubility with low dermal absorption and low systemic bioavailability, and that genotoxic potential was not expected [4]. It concluded the substances can be considered safe up to a combined 10 percent, excluding spray or aerosol products, because no safe level could be set for inhalation given possible lung effects, and it noted a lack of validated methods to determine the composition of products containing them [4]. The group also said that extrapolating toxicological data from the non-nano to the nano form was inappropriate and that its assessment applied to particles above 50 nm median by number [4].

A study of healthy volunteers with Fitzpatrick skin types II to IV irradiated the lower back with narrow-band 385 nm and 405 nm light at increasing doses and reported that a new visible-light-absorbing organic filter gave superior protection against pigmentation at the ultraviolet-visible boundary [2]. No trials of consumer sunscreens containing HAA299 for long-term skin outcomes were found.
